rows.label: Concept
rows.text: For constant acceleration, three equations connect u, v, a, t and s — and the velocity–time graph derives all of them. The **slope** of the v–t line gives $a = (v-u)/t$, i.e. $v = u + at$; the **area** splits into a rectangle $ut$ and a triangle $\frac{1}{2}at^2$, giving $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$; the total area $\frac{u+v}{2}t$ rearranges to $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.…

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Uniform velocity vs uniform acceleration:** uniform velocity means a = 0 (v–t graph horizontal); uniform acceleration means the v–t graph is a straight sloped line.  ·  **Distance vs displacement in these equations:** the equations give displacement; total path length needs separate handling when direction reverses.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Note 1: Always draw and label the $v$–$t$ graph in derivation questions — the diagram itself carries marks.  ·  Note 2: For two-stage journeys (accelerate then brake), apply the equations to EACH stage and add the areas.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Verified PYQs: car numerical (2023, 3m; 2014, 3m). The graphical derivation itself is a standard theory question.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Task 1: Perform all three graphical derivations with a single labelled figure, from memory.  ·  Task 2: Solve ten numericals classifying them by which equation fits (u/v/a/t/s given-asked table).

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): A train decelerates uniformly from 30 m/s to rest in 150 m. Find the deceleration and the time taken.** — v² = u² + 2as → 0 = 900 − 2a(150) → a = 3 m/s² (deceleration); t = (v−u)/a = 30/3 = 10 s.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Most-tested: two-equation numericals (2014, 2023). Be ready to draw and label the v–t graph for the derivation.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Graphs are derivations:** slope gives a, area gives s — the three equations are geometry on the v–t plane.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: v = u + at (slope of v–t line); s = ut + ½at² (rectangle + triangle area); v² = u² + 2as (average-velocity area).  ·  Choose the equation by which quantity is absent: no t → v² = u² + 2as; no s → v = u + at; no v → s = ut + ½at².

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The third equation lets you find stopping distance without knowing the braking time — the basis of road-safety calculations.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Three Equations from Two Graphs For motion with **constant acceleration**, three equations connect the five quantities u, v, a, t, s. The graphical derivation — reading slopes and areas off the velocity–time graph — shows where they come from without calculus, and is itself the examinable derivation.  ·  ## 2. The Three Equations of Motion | Equation | Links | Use when asked for | |---|---|---| | $v = u + at$ | v, u, a, t | velocity after time t (no s) | | $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ | s, u, a, t | displacement after time t (no v) | | $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ | v, u, a, s | displacement without time (no t) | ### 2.1 Graphical derivation (the examinable one) Draw the velocity–time…  ·  ## 4. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 6:** the equations are the integrals of $a = dv/dt$ for constant a; the graphical derivation is the pre-calculus version. - **To Topic 9:** free fall is these equations with a = g, u = 0 (dropped) or u = 0 downward, and sign conventions.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Note 3: Convert km/h to m/s before substituting (divide by 3.6) — the most common numerical slip.  ·  Note 4: If the body reverses direction, compute each leg separately and add magnitudes for distance, not displacement.  ·  "Slope and area: the v–t graph holds all three equations."

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Why does the third equation have no time term?  ·  Task 3: Verify $s_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n-1)$ by computing $s(n) - s(n-1)$ explicitly.  ·  Task 4: Solve a two-stage train problem (accelerate, cruise, brake) via the $v$–$t$ area method.
